meta.blurb: A boy raised by wolves, a bear who teaches the Law, a panther who loves him and a tiger who wants him. Follow Mowgli, brave little Rikki-Tikki-Tavi and a boy called Toomai through Kipling's jungle. Can the man-cub find where he belongs?
meta.bible: Mowgli: the man-cub, called the Frog, raised by wolves in the Seeonee hills of India. Father Wolf and Mother Wolf: the wolves who take Mowgli in; they have four cubs. Akela: the old grey leader of the Seeonee Pack. Gray Brother: the eldest of Mother Wolf's cubs and Mowgli's faithful friend. Shere Khan: the great tiger, lame from birth, who hunts Mowgli and fears fire. Tabaqui: the sly jackal who carries tales. Baloo: the sleepy old brown bear who teaches the Law of the Jungle. Bagheera: the sleek black panther who buys Mowgli's place in the Pack with a bull. Kaa: the huge rock python who helps against the monkeys and does the Dance of Hunger. Bandar-log: the Monkey People, who have no Law, no leader and no memory. Chil: the kite, a bird who carries the news. Cold Lairs: the ruined city where the monkeys take Mowgli. Council Rock: the flat rock where the Pack meets. Red Flower: the jungle's name for fire. Law of the Jungle: the rules every jungle animal keeps. Rikki-Tikki-Tavi: a young mongoose, washed out by a flood, adopted by an English family in India. Teddy: the family's small son; his father and mother live in the bungalow. Darzee: a brave tailorbird who lives in the garden. Nag: a great black cobra. Nagaina: his wife. Their eggs are hidden in the melon bed. Kala Nag: the old working elephant, Black Snake. Little Toomai: a ten-year-old boy whose father and family drive elephants; he sees the elephants dance and is named Toomai of the Elephants. Messua: the kind village woman whose small son was carried off long ago by a tiger. Rama: the great bull who leads the village buffaloes. Seeonee. India. Kipling's four stories: Mowgli's Brothers, Kaa's Hunting, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi (beats 23-31), Toomai of the Elephants, Tiger! Tiger! Voice and tone: warm, adventurous and a little wild, like a story told by a fire. Dangers are real but never gory: deaths are stated plainly and gently; the tiger dies when the buffalo herd stampedes.

beats.scene: Father Wolf wakes in his cave on a green hillside at sunset
beats.summary: At dusk in the Seeonee hills, Father Wolf wakes beside Mother Wolf and their four cubs.

beats.scene: A thin jackal peeps into the cave mouth at dusk
beats.summary: Tabaqui the jackal arrives with news that Shere Khan the tiger has come to hunt in the Pack's hills.

beats.scene: A huge tiger roars angrily in the dark jungle below the cave
beats.summary: Shere Khan roars in the dark below the cave, angry that his hunt has failed.

beats.scene: A small brown baby crawls into the cave and laughs at the wolves
beats.summary: A human baby crawls into the cave, and Mother Wolf decides to keep him and names him Mowgli the Frog.

beats.scene: Shere Khan's huge head fills the cave mouth while Mother Wolf glares back
beats.summary: Shere Khan demands the child, but Mother Wolf refuses fiercely and he leaves, swearing to return.

beats.scene: Wolves gather in a ring around a great flat rock under the moon
beats.summary: Father Wolf carries Mowgli to Council Rock to show him to the whole Pack and its leader, Akela.

beats.scene: Baloo the old brown bear stands up to speak before the wolves
beats.summary: Shere Khan claims the child, and Baloo the bear, who teaches the Law, rises to speak for him.

beats.scene: Bagheera the black panther lays a fresh bull before the Pack
beats.summary: Bagheera buys Mowgli's life with a freshly killed bull, and the Pack accepts the boy.

beats.scene: Mowgli plays with wolf cubs while Baloo teaches him beside a stream
beats.summary: Mowgli grows up among the wolves, and Baloo teaches him the Law of the Jungle and its Master-Words.

beats.scene: Mowgli runs through the dark jungle carrying a clay pot of glowing coals
beats.summary: Bagheera warns Mowgli of danger, and Mowgli fetches the Red Flower, fire, from the village of men.

beats.scene: Old Akela lies tired on the rock after a missed hunt
beats.summary: Akela misses a kill, and Shere Khan stirs the young wolves against both Akela and Mowgli.

beats.scene: Mowgli holds a burning branch before snarling Shere Khan
beats.summary: Mowgli swings a burning branch, drives Shere Khan away and shields Akela.

beats.scene: Mowgli weeps beside Mother Wolf and his wolf brothers at the cave
beats.summary: Mowgli decides to leave the Pack, weeps for the first time and promises to bring back the tiger's skin.

beats.scene: Baloo scolds Mowgli beneath a tree while monkeys chatter above
beats.summary: Living with Baloo and Bagheera, Mowgli is warned to keep away from the lawless Monkey People.

beats.scene: Monkeys carry Mowgli across the treetops high above the jungle
beats.summary: While Mowgli sleeps, the monkeys snatch him and swing away with him through the treetops.

beats.scene: Mowgli calls up to Chil the kite circling in the blue sky
beats.summary: Mowgli calls to Chil the kite, who flies off to tell Baloo and Bagheera where he has been taken.

beats.scene: Baloo and Bagheera hurry along a jungle path as the kite guides them
beats.summary: Chil brings the news, and Bagheera says that only Kaa the rock python can frighten the monkeys.

beats.scene: Kaa the huge rock python rests on a sunny rock as Bagheera bows
beats.summary: Kaa the python, who loves hunting monkeys, agrees to help after Bagheera speaks to him with respect.

beats.scene: Mowgli sits among chattering monkeys in a crumbling stone city
beats.summary: In the Cold Lairs, the monkeys keep Mowgli among the ruins and pester him.

beats.scene: Bagheera leaps among a swarm of monkeys while Baloo fights beside him
beats.summary: Bagheera and Baloo reach the ruins first and are swamped by the huge crowd of monkeys.

beats.scene: Kaa sways before a crowd of monkeys frozen in silence
beats.summary: Kaa arrives and begins the Dance of Hunger, and the monkeys stand frozen and stare.

beats.scene: Mowgli, Baloo and Bagheera walk away from the ruins at dawn
beats.summary: Kaa breaks down a wall to free Mowgli, the monkeys scatter, and the friends go home.

beats.scene: A small wet mongoose lies in the grass of a garden after a flood
beats.summary: A flood washes a young mongoose, Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, into a garden, where an English family finds and saves him.

beats.scene: Rikki-Tikki runs along a table and peers into a bungalow bathroom
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki explores the bungalow, and Teddy's father says a mongoose is a useful friend in a garden full of snakes.

beats.scene: Darzee the tailorbird cries beside his leaf nest in a bush
beats.summary: In the garden Rikki-Tikki meets Darzee the tailorbird, who says Nag and Nagaina the cobras are hunting near his nest.

beats.scene: Nag the cobra rears up with his hood spread wide in the grass
beats.summary: Nag rises from the grass to frighten Rikki-Tikki, but the little mongoose stands his ground.

beats.scene: At night Nag glides into a dark bathroom while Rikki-Tikki waits
beats.summary: That night Nag creeps into the bathroom to wait for the family, and Rikki-Tikki lies in wait for him.

beats.scene: Rikki-Tikki bites the cobra's hood as Teddy's father raises a gun
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki seizes Nag and holds on, and Teddy's father ends the fight; Nag is dead.

beats.scene: Nagaina the cobra hisses beside a garden wall and plans revenge
beats.summary: Nagaina swears revenge, and Rikki-Tikki knows he must find her eggs hidden in the melon bed.

beats.scene: Nagaina rears behind Teddy at the breakfast table while Rikki-Tikki watches
beats.summary: Nagaina threatens Teddy at breakfast, and Rikki-Tikki draws her away by showing her one of her eggs.

beats.scene: Rikki-Tikki chases a cobra into a hole in the garden
beats.summary: Rikki-Tikki leads Nagaina to the melon bed, then follows her into her hole, and the cobras never trouble the garden again.

beats.scene: Little Toomai sits on the neck of the great elephant Kala Nag
beats.summary: Little Toomai, a ten-year-old whose family drives elephants, adores the old elephant Kala Nag.

beats.scene: Old hunters sit by a campfire at night, talking about dancing elephants
beats.summary: The old hunters speak of a secret elephant dance that no man has seen, and Toomai's father says the boy must see it first.

beats.scene: Little Toomai lies against Kala Nag as the elephant pulls his chain
beats.summary: That night Kala Nag pulls loose from his chain and walks away, and Little Toomai climbs onto his neck.

beats.scene: Kala Nag walks through a dark jungle with other elephants beside him
beats.summary: They walk all night through the jungle, and more elephants join them out of the dark.

beats.scene: Many elephants stamp in circles in a moonlit clearing on a hilltop
beats.summary: On a bare hilltop the elephants dance in the moonlight while Little Toomai watches.

beats.scene: The camp cheers at dawn as Little Toomai returns on Kala Nag
beats.summary: At dawn Kala Nag carries Little Toomai home, the hunters find the dancing ground, and the boy is named Toomai of the Elephants.

beats.scene: Mother Wolf holds Mowgli's face gently at the cave door at evening
beats.summary: Mowgli, now older, wonders where he belongs, and Mother Wolf tells him that he must one day live among men.

beats.scene: Messua opens her arms to a ragged boy at a village hut door
beats.summary: At the village, Messua, whose small son was carried off by a tiger long ago, takes Mowgli into her house.

beats.scene: Mowgli sits on a buffalo's back in a hot field with village boys
beats.summary: Mowgli learns the ways of the village and herds the buffaloes with the other boys.

beats.scene: Gray Brother crouches in the grass at dusk and whispers to Mowgli
beats.summary: Gray Brother warns Mowgli that Shere Khan is waiting in the ravine near the village.

beats.scene: Mowgli and Gray Brother plan beside the village buffaloes in the evening
beats.summary: Mowgli plans to use the buffalo herd and sends Gray Brother to fetch Akela to help.

beats.scene: Mowgli rides a great bull while two wolves gather the herd on a hillside
beats.summary: At first light Mowgli leads the herd to the head of the ravine while Akela and Gray Brother split it in two.

beats.scene: A buffalo herd thunders down a narrow rocky valley in a dust cloud
beats.summary: Mowgli calls out, the herd charges down the ravine, and Shere Khan is trapped and killed.

beats.scene: Mowgli stands in the quiet ravine beside the tiger's striped skin
beats.summary: Mowgli takes Shere Khan's skin, as he promised he would, and prepares to carry it away.

beats.scene: Angry village men with sticks shout at Mowgli at the edge of the field
beats.summary: The villagers see the tiger's skin, call Mowgli a sorcerer, throw stones and drive him away.

beats.scene: Mowgli walks alone out of the village carrying a tiger skin at dusk
beats.summary: Sad but unafraid, Mowgli leaves the village with the skin and heads back toward the jungle.

beats.scene: Mowgli spreads the striped tiger skin on the great flat Council Rock
beats.summary: Mowgli spreads the skin on Council Rock and calls the Pack together.

beats.scene: Wolves sit in a circle around the tiger skin while Mowgli sings
beats.summary: The wolves welcome Mowgli and ask him to lead them; he refuses, preferring to run with them as a brother.

beats.scene: Mowgli runs through the moonlit jungle with his wolf brothers
beats.summary: Mowgli settles back into the jungle among his brothers and friends, and the story ends in peace.

A1A2: Father Wolf woke up in his cave when the sun went down.
A thin wild dog called Tabaqui came to the cave.
Shere Khan roared outside, because his hunt in the night had failed.
A small brown baby crawled into the cave, and Mother Wolf named him Mowgli.
The tiger wanted the baby, but Mother Wolf said no.
Father Wolf took the baby to a big rock where the wolves met.
Baloo, the old brown bear, said the child was his friend.
Bagheera the black panther paid for the boy with food, and the Pack said yes.
Mowgli grew up with the wolf cubs and learned the jungle.
Bagheera warned Mowgli, so Mowgli took fire from the village.
Old Akela missed his kill, and the young wolves were angry.
Mowgli held up the fire, and Shere Khan was afraid.
Mowgli cried and said goodbye to his wolf family.
Baloo told Mowgli to stay away from the monkeys.
The monkeys took Mowgli and jumped through the trees.
Mowgli called to a bird, and the bird went to find help.
Bagheera said that only Kaa the big snake could help.
Kaa, the long snake, said yes and went with them.
The monkeys kept Mowgli in an old city with broken walls.
Bagheera and Baloo fought the monkeys, but there were too many.
Kaa came and moved slowly, and the monkeys could not move.
Kaa helped free Mowgli, and the monkeys all ran away.
A flood carried a small animal called Rikki-Tikki-Tavi into a garden.
Rikki-Tikki ran about the house and looked at everything.
A small bird told Rikki about two bad snakes.
Nag lifted his head high and looked at Rikki.
At night, Nag went into the house, and Rikki waited.
Rikki held Nag, and Teddy's father shot the snake.
Nagaina was very angry, and she wanted to hurt the family.
Rikki took an egg and made Nagaina come after him.
Rikki followed Nagaina into her hole, and the garden was safe.
Little Toomai was a boy who loved a big elephant.
The men said that elephants dance in the dark.
That night, Kala Nag left the camp, and Toomai rode him.
They walked far, and other elephants came out of the dark.
Many elephants walked in a big circle in the moonlight.
At dawn the men gave Toomai a new name, Toomai of the Elephants.
Mother Wolf said that Mowgli should live with people.
A kind woman named Messua took Mowgli into her home.
Mowgli learned the village ways and looked after the buffalo.
Gray Brother came to Mowgli and said that Shere Khan was near.
Mowgli had a plan, and the buffalo would help him.
The next morning, the wolves and Mowgli drove the buffalo.
Shere Khan was dead, and he would never hurt anyone again.
Mowgli took the tiger's skin and carried it away.
The village men were afraid of Mowgli and sent him away.
Mowgli left the village and walked back to the jungle.
Mowgli put the tiger's skin on the big rock.
The wolves were happy, and they asked Mowgli to be their leader.
Mowgli ran with his wolf brothers, and the jungle was his home again.
B1B2: In the Seeonee hills it was a warm evening, and Father Wolf was just waking up. Beside him lay Mother Wolf with their four small cubs.
Tabaqui the jackal, a sly beggar whom nobody liked, peeped into the cave and asked for food. Then he said that Shere Khan, the great tiger, had decided to hunt on their side of the hills.

Outside the cave, Shere Khan's roar rolled through the dark, for he had missed his prey and hurt his foot. Father Wolf listened and frowned, because the tiger was hunting in the wrong place and breaking the rules of the jungle.
Then a small brown baby, lost from his human parents, crawled into the cave and laughed up at the wolves. Mother Wolf decided to keep him and called him Mowgli, which means the Frog.

Soon Shere Khan's great head appeared at the cave mouth, and he demanded the little human that had run in there. Mother Wolf, her eyes blazing like green moons, answered that the boy was hers and she would never give him up.

The Pack met on a great flat rock, called Council Rock, whenever something important had to be decided. Father Wolf carried Mowgli there so that Akela, the grey leader, and all the wolves could accept the child.
Shere Khan roared that the child belonged to him, and some of the young wolves wanted to give the boy up. Then Baloo, the old brown bear who taught the Law of the Jungle, stood up and spoke for him.
Next, Bagheera the black panther offered a fat bull that he had just killed as the price of the boy's life. The hungry wolves agreed at once, and Mowgli became a member of the Seeonee Pack.
For ten or eleven years Mowgli grew up with the wolf cubs, running and hunting beside them. Baloo taught him the Law of the Jungle and the words that all the jungle folk know.

Bagheera warned Mowgli that Akela was growing old and that Shere Khan was already whispering to the young wolves. So Mowgli ran to a village, took a pot of glowing coals from a hut, and carried the Red Flower home.

One night old Akela missed his kill, and by the Law of the Pack he had to give up his place. Shere Khan, who waited nearby, whispered to the young wolves that they should be rid of both Akela and the man-cub.
Mowgli walked into the circle and lit a branch from his pot of fire, and the wolves drew back in fear. He drove Shere Khan away with the flames and stood in front of Akela to protect him.

Mowgli knew that the Pack was no longer safe for him, so he said goodbye to Mother Wolf and his wolf brothers. For the first time in his life he wept, and he promised that one day he would lay Shere Khan's skin on the Council Rock.
Mowgli now lived in the jungle with Baloo and Bagheera, and he was still learning from them every day. Baloo warned him to stay away from the monkeys, who have no Law, no leader and no memory.

One afternoon, while Mowgli lay asleep, a crowd of monkeys seized him and swung away through the treetops. They shrieked that he was clever and that he must teach them how to weave branches into walls.
High in the sky Mowgli saw Chil the kite, and he called out a greeting that every bird understands. Chil promised to follow the monkeys and to tell Baloo and Bagheera where the boy had been taken.
Chil gave Baloo and Bagheera the news, and the two friends set off at once through the jungle. Bagheera said that the monkeys fear only Kaa the rock python, so they went to ask him for help.
They found Kaa lying in the sun with his newly changed skin glistening, and Bagheera greeted him with great respect. The huge python was hungry, and he was glad to help them against the monkeys.
In the old ruined city the monkeys danced and shouted around Mowgli, and they promised him many wonderful things. Mowgli was hungry and tired, but he kept calm and waited for his friends.
Bagheera and Baloo arrived first, and they fought bravely to reach Mowgli. However, the monkeys were so many that the two friends were soon covered and could hardly move.
Then Kaa arrived and began to sway slowly from side to side. The monkeys stared into his shining eyes and could not look away, and they forgot how to run.
Kaa broke through the old wall and set Mowgli free, and the frightened monkeys fled in every direction. Mowgli thanked the great snake, and then he went home with his friends, wiser than before.
After a great flood, a young mongoose called Rikki-Tikki-Tavi was found lying in a ditch by an English family in India. Teddy, the small son, carried him home, dried him and let him sleep in his bed.
Rikki-Tikki ran all over the house, sniffed every corner and even climbed onto the table. Teddy's father said that he would be a useful friend, because a mongoose is the enemy of every snake.
In the garden Rikki-Tikki met Darzee the tailorbird, who was crying beside his nest. Darzee said that a cobra named Nag, and Nag's wife Nagaina, had been hunting near his babies.
Nag rose slowly out of the grass, spread his wide hood and tried to frighten the small mongoose. Rikki-Tikki felt a cold shiver, but his eyes turned red and he refused to run away.
That night Nag glided into the dark bathroom, planning to harm the humans when they came in the morning. Rikki-Tikki, who had been watching quietly, understood at once and decided that he must act.
Rikki-Tikki jumped and bit Nag behind the hood, holding on while the cobra whipped him against the floor. Teddy's father ran in with a gun and ended the fight, and Nag died.

The next morning Nagaina, who was now alone and full of rage, promised to take her revenge on the whole family. Rikki-Tikki knew that her eggs lay hidden in the melon bed, so he went quietly to look for them.
Nagaina crept onto the veranda where Teddy sat, ready to strike him. Rikki-Tikki ran in with one of her eggs in his mouth, and the cobra turned to him at once.

Rikki-Tikki raced for the melon bed with Nagaina behind him, while Darzee fluttered in her face to confuse her. After a long fight in the dark hole, Rikki-Tikki came out alone, and the cobras never troubled the garden again.

Little Toomai was a ten-year-old boy in India, and he loved Kala Nag, the great elephant that his father rode. His family had cared for elephants for many generations, and the boy dreamed of becoming a famous driver himself.

One night the old hunters talked about a secret dance of the wild elephants, but nobody had ever seen it. Little Toomai's father laughed and said that the boy would be a real driver on the day he saw the dance himself.
Later that night Kala Nag broke his chain and walked quietly away from the camp. Little Toomai, who was lying awake beside him, climbed onto the great neck, and the elephant did not seem to mind.

All night they pushed through the thick jungle, and more elephants came quietly out of the dark. Little Toomai heard their soft footsteps all around him, and he felt afraid, although he did not want to turn back.

On a hilltop the herd stopped in a wide, bare clearing, and the elephants began to stamp, hour after hour. The ground shook under Little Toomai, and he knew that he was seeing what no man in the camp had ever seen.
At dawn Kala Nag carried the tired boy home, where the hunters listened to his story with wide eyes. From that day the men called him Toomai of the Elephants, and they told his story for years.

More years passed, and Mowgli grew into a strong, thoughtful boy who often wondered where he truly belonged. Mother Wolf told him that Shere Khan still waited for him and that he must one day live among men.

At the edge of the village a kind woman named Messua stared at Mowgli and then took him into her house. Long ago a tiger had carried off her small son, and she hoped that this boy was the child she had lost.

In the village Mowgli learned to speak with people and to wear clothes, although everything seemed strange. Each day he took the village buffaloes out to the grass with the other boys, and he found the work easy.

One evening Gray Brother, the eldest of Mowgli's wolf brothers, crept out of the grass to speak with him. He warned Mowgli that Shere Khan was waiting in the ravine nearby and meant to catch him when he came home.

Mowgli decided to use the buffalo herd, because nothing in the jungle can stand against a charging herd. He sent Gray Brother to fetch old Akela, and the three of them planned how to drive the animals into the ravine.

At dawn Mowgli rode the leader of the herd to the top of the ravine, and the wolves ran along beside him. Akela and Gray Brother cut the herd in two, so that the animals could be driven down from both ends of the valley.

Mowgli called out Shere Khan's name, and the whole herd thundered down the narrow valley like a great wave of horns and dust. The tiger was trapped between the two halves, and when the dust settled, he was dead.
When the dust had settled, Mowgli took Shere Khan's skin with his knife, as hunters do. He had said long ago that the tiger's skin would lie on the Council Rock, and he meant to keep his word.
When Mowgli went back to the village, a hunter saw the tiger's skin and shouted that the boy was a sorcerer. The frightened villagers threw stones, and Mowgli had to run away.

Mowgli felt a sharp sadness, because Messua had been kind to him and he had hoped to stay among men. However, he lifted the skin onto his shoulder and walked back toward the jungle, where he knew that he was wanted.

At dawn Mowgli reached Council Rock and spread the tiger's skin across the stones, holding it down with heavy sticks. Then he called the Pack together, and the wolves came running from every part of the hills.
The wolves cheered when they saw the skin, and the Pack asked Mowgli to be their new leader. Mowgli thanked them, but he said that he would rather be their brother than their master.

From that day Mowgli ran with his wolf brothers through the moonlit forest, as happy as he had ever been. Shere Khan was gone, his friends were close, and the jungle that had raised him was his home once more.
C1C2: At the end of a sultry Indian day, Father Wolf stirred in his cave on the Seeonee hills, scratched himself and yawned the sleep out of his jaws. Beside him lay Mother Wolf, grey and watchful, with her four tumbling cubs pressed against her flank. Outside, the jungle was beginning to wake, and the dusk was full of rustling and distant calls.

Presently a shadow fell across the cave mouth, and Tabaqui the jackal, a sly little beggar whom the whole jungle despised, sidled in to ask for a bone. He was a tale-bearer and a trouble-maker, and he took great pleasure in carrying bad news from one lair to the next. This evening he whispered, with a sneer, that Shere Khan, the great striped tiger, had changed his hunting grounds and now meant to hunt among these very hills.

Not long afterwards a low, whining roar rolled up the hillside, the angry complaint of a tiger who had gone hungry and hurt his foot in the dark. Father Wolf listened with a frown, for he knew that Shere Khan, who had been lame from birth, had no business hunting on their ground and was making enough noise to warn every deer in the jungle. In the thicket below, the great cat could be heard crashing about and growling to himself.

Out of the darkness a small, brown, naked child crept on hands and knees into the cave, plucked at Father Wolf's fur and laughed as if the wolves were old friends. Mother Wolf, who loved all small things, felt her heart go out to him and declared that she would keep him for her own. She named him Mowgli the Frog and promised that he should grow up among her four cubs.

Soon the great head of Shere Khan blocked the cave mouth, and his hungry, angry voice demanded the little human creature that had strayed into the wolves' home. Mother Wolf rose up with her eyes blazing like two green moons in the dark, and she answered that the child was hers, to be kept, and that no lame killer would ever lay a tooth on him. Too large to squeeze through the narrow opening, the tiger could only roar his fury and promise that the child would be his in the end.

By old custom, every cub had to be shown to the whole Pack before it was counted as one of them, so Father Wolf carried Mowgli to the Council Rock. There the wolves had gathered in a ring around Akela, the great grey leader who had ruled them by strength and cunning for many years. Shere Khan was already waiting among the shadows, ready to claim the child for himself.

Shere Khan thrust himself forward and demanded the man-cub as his rightful prey, and a few wolves, afraid of his bad temper, began to murmur that the child should be given up. Then Baloo, the sleepy old bear who taught the wolf cubs the Law of the Jungle, rose on his hind legs and offered to speak in the boy's defence. His slow, deep voice filled the hollow, and the whole Pack fell silent to hear it.

Then Bagheera, the sleek black panther, glided into the circle and offered a fat young bull he had killed that evening as the price of the boy's life. The hungry Pack, reminded that by old custom a cub's place could be bought, growled their agreement, and Shere Khan stalked away into the night, snarling that he would be back. So Mowgli the man-cub was accepted into the Seeonee Pack, and he began his life as one more cub in the family of Father Wolf and Mother Wolf.

Year after year Mowgli grew up among the wolf cubs, learning to run, to climb and to listen, until he knew every path and every sound of the jungle as well as any wolf. Baloo, the patient old bear, taught him the Law of the Jungle and the Master-Words that win the respect of every creature, from the snake to the kite. Between lessons Mowgli played in the river and slept in the sun, as happy as a boy could be.

When Bagheera warned that Akela was growing old and that Shere Khan was already whispering poison into the ears of the younger wolves, Mowgli understood that the day of danger was near. Following the panther's advice, he ran through the dusk to a village of men, slipped into a hut and took a clay pot of glowing coals from the hearth. He carried the Red Flower home through the dark jungle, feeding it with dry sticks as he went, and he laughed to see it live in his hands.

At last the evil day came, when old Akela missed his kill, and by the hard Law of the Pack a leader who failed was no longer fit to lead. Shere Khan, who had been waiting in the shadows for exactly this moment, crept among the younger wolves and fed their ambitions with flattery, until they were ready to be rid of both Akela and the man-cub. A great meeting was called at the Council Rock, and all the wolves gathered in the moonlight to decide.

Mowgli strode into the ring of wolves, thrust a dry branch into the pot until it blazed, and swung the flame before him so that the whole Pack shrank back from the Red Flower. Shere Khan, who feared fire above all things, flinched and whimpered, and he was driven from the Rock with his tail between his legs, while Mowgli stood protectively beside Akela. The wolves, awed by the Red Flower, murmured that the man-cub held a power that no wolf could match.

Though he had saved Akela, Mowgli knew that his place in the Pack was gone, for Shere Khan's whispers had done their work and the young wolves no longer trusted a boy who carried fire. He said farewell to Mother Wolf and to his brothers, and for the first time in his life hot tears ran down his face, a thing that astonished him. Wiping them away, he vowed that he would return one day with Shere Khan's skin to lay upon the Council Rock.

In the weeks that followed, Mowgli stayed close to his two teachers, and Baloo, who took his lessons very seriously, soon felt the need to warn him against the Monkey People. They were chattering, quarrelsome creatures who lived in the treetops, had no Law, no leader and no memory, and boasted endlessly of great deeds that they promptly forgot. The jungle folk never spoke of them, and no respectable animal would be seen in their company.

One drowsy afternoon, while Baloo dozed nearby, a chattering mob of monkeys seized Mowgli by the arms and legs and swung him away over the swaying treetops, faster than any boy could run. They screamed to one another that he was clever and wonderful, that he would teach them to weave branches into walls, and that this would make them the greatest people in the jungle. Dizzy and furious, Mowgli clung on and wondered how far from his friends he was being taken.

High above the treetops, Mowgli caught sight of Chil the kite, circling lazily on the wind, and he shouted up the Master-Word of the kite people, which was a promise of friendship between hunters. Chil dipped at once, for the jungle folk respect that call, and swore to follow the monkeys all the way and to carry the news to Baloo and Bagheera. Then the great bird rose on the warm air and sped across the jungle without a moment to lose.

Chil brought the news to Baloo and Bagheera, who sprang up in alarm and began to race through the undergrowth towards the ruined city where the monkeys had gone. The panther, who knew the jungle better than any creature, said that the Monkey People feared only one animal, Kaa the great rock python, whose hunger was famous. Since two friends alone could not defeat a whole tribe, they agreed to seek out the huge snake and beg him to lend his strength.

Kaa, thirty feet of glittering muscle, had just shed his old skin and lay basking on a warm rock, and Bagheera, who was always wary of him, greeted him with the soft words a hunter owes a hunter. When he heard that the monkeys had taken a man-cub and had never shown any respect to the python, Kaa's eyes brightened, for he was hungry and the Monkey People were his favourite game. In the end he agreed to go with them to the old ruined city where the monkeys had gone.

The monkeys carried Mowgli into the Cold Lairs, an abandoned city of broken walls, empty halls and crumbling palaces, and there they danced round him, boasting and quarrelling and tugging at his hair. The boy was hungry, tired and sick of being pushed about, but he kept his temper and waited, telling himself that his friends would not be long. All around him the moon rose over the ruins, and the monkeys shrieked louder than ever.

Bagheera and Baloo reached the ruins before Kaa and charged in at once, the panther striking left and right with his powerful paws while the bear lumbered through the crowd. The monkeys, who were hundreds strong, swarmed over them from the walls and roofs, biting and pulling, until the two friends were buried beneath a heap of chattering bodies. Even so, Bagheera shouted to Mowgli to keep his courage, for help was near.

Then Kaa slid out of the darkness and, rocking his great head from side to side, began the slow, hypnotic movement known as the Dance of Hunger. The monkeys, who had screamed with such confidence a moment before, stood rooted to the spot, staring into his unwinking eyes and shuffling forward as if in a dream. Even Bagheera had to look away, and he whispered to Mowgli not to meet the python's gaze.

Kaa's great body crashed against the crumbling wall and brought it down, and Mowgli, free at last, hurried out through the gap to the safety of his friends. The monkeys, shaken from their trance, scattered in terror across the ruins and did not trouble the jungle for a long time. Mowgli thanked the huge snake warmly and then, with Baloo and Bagheera beside him, walked home in the early light, a little wiser than before.

When the summer rains had swept a young mongoose called Rikki-Tikki-Tavi away from his burrow, he was washed down a ditch into a garden in India, where an English boy named Teddy found him half drowned in the grass. The family took him into their bungalow, dried him by the fire and wrapped him in cotton wool, and by morning the little creature was sitting up and demanding breakfast. He was a lively, fearless little animal, and from that day on he belonged to the family.

Nothing escaped Rikki-Tikki's attention, for curiosity was the whole creed of his family, and he scampered over tables, peered into the bath and even poked his nose into the ink on the writing desk. Teddy's father laughed and said that a mongoose in the garden would be worth a great deal, since the grounds were full of snakes. Within a day the little creature had won the hearts of everyone in the house, and he was as happy as a mongoose can be.

Out in the garden Rikki-Tikki met Darzee the tailorbird, who sat sobbing beside the nest he and his wife had sewn out of leaves, and who could only moan that nothing in the garden was safe. A great black cobra named Nag, he explained, lived in the grass with his wife Nagaina, and the two of them had been prowling around the nest and its little chicks for days. Rikki-Tikki, though only a small mongoose, was not frightened, for his mother had taught him that fighting snakes was the work of his family.

A hiss came from the long grass, and Nag, the black cobra, rose slowly out of it until his spread hood towered above the tiny mongoose, swaying and glittering in the sun. He said, in his cold, soft voice, that he was an old and terrible snake and that Rikki would do well to leave the garden. Rikki-Tikki felt a chill pass through him, but his eyes turned as red as hot coals, his fur bristled and he stood his ground.

In the dead of night Nag slid through a drain into the bungalow and coiled himself in the dark bathroom, planning to strike at the humans when they came in the morning. Rikki-Tikki, who had been watching quietly from the shadows, understood the danger at once and decided that no one else must be left to meet it. He crept closer, step by step, and waited for the right moment to spring.

Rikki-Tikki sprang the moment Nag's head touched the floor, sank his teeth into the back of the hood and held on grimly while the cobra lashed him to and fro like a whip. Roused by the noise, Teddy's father hurried in with a gun and ended the fight with a single shot. Nag lay dead, and Rikki-Tikki, bruised from head to tail but very proud, was the hero of the household.

When she learned that her husband was dead, Nagaina slid through the grass in a terrible rage and swore that she would have her revenge on Rikki-Tikki and the people he served. Rikki understood that a mother cobra would do anything for her eggs, and he remembered that a great many of them lay hidden in the melon bed at the end of the garden. He went quietly down the path, leaving Darzee to watch the house, and he knew that he must reach them before the baby snakes hatched.

While the family sat at breakfast on the veranda, Nagaina glided silently up behind Teddy's chair, her hood spread, ready to strike the boy and make the whole household pay for her husband's death. At that very moment Rikki-Tikki dashed in with one of her eggs between his teeth and warned her that the rest would not be safe if she touched the child. Teddy's father snatched the boy out of reach, and the cobra, forgetting everything else, turned on the mongoose and begged him for her egg.

Rikki-Tikki raced towards the melon bed with Nagaina close behind, while Darzee, who bravely pretended to be hurt, led her off along the path and never let her catch him. At last the cobra slid into her hole, and Rikki-Tikki, drawing a deep breath, followed her into the darkness. Many minutes later he came out alone, tired but victorious, and the garden knew that the cobras would trouble it no more.

In the hills of India, a boy named Little Toomai lived in an elephant catchers' camp, and nothing mattered to him half as much as Kala Nag, the huge old elephant his father drove. For generations his family had served the Government in capturing and training elephants, and the child had grown up between those great grey legs, learning their ways before he could read. He longed to become a driver himself, though his father insisted that he must first learn the patience that the work demands.

Round the camp fire one night, the old hunters spoke softly of the secret dance that wild elephants were said to hold in hidden clearings, where the ground was trodden as hard as stone. Nobody in the camp had ever seen it, and nobody who had gone looking had come back with a clear story to tell. When the boy begged to join the next hunt, his father laughed and answered that Toomai could become a real driver only after he had seen the elephants dance.

In the small hours, when every man lay asleep, Kala Nag tugged his heavy chain loose and moved off towards the dark hills, his great feet making no more noise than a breeze. Little Toomai, who had been lying awake beside him, caught hold of the elephant's ear, scrambled up the great trunk and settled himself on the broad neck as quietly as a mouse. The old elephant paused for a moment, as if to see whether the boy was serious, and then he went on.

Hour after hour they pushed through the thick jungle, and one by one the great shapes of other elephants slipped out of the darkness and fell in beside Kala Nag. Little Toomai could hear the brushing of vast bodies against the bushes, the soft rumble of their voices and the slow tread of feet that seemed to know exactly where they were going. He was afraid, yet he gripped the thick ear and would not have turned back for anything in the world.

At last the herd reached a wide, bare hilltop where the earth had been stamped as hard as stone by countless generations of feet, and there, under the moon, the elephants began to dance. They stamped and trampled in great slow circles, trumpeting softly, while the ground shook beneath Little Toomai and the trees trembled all around the clearing. He clung to Kala Nag's neck with his heart pounding, knowing that he was watching what no man in the camp had seen with his own eyes.

By sunrise Kala Nag had walked back to the camp with Little Toomai asleep on his neck, and the hunters, who had searched for the boy all night, listened to his tale with wonder. They followed the trail and found the vast trampled clearing in the forest, and they knew that the boy had told the truth. From that day the people of the hills called him Toomai of the Elephants, and they told his story for many years.

As the seasons turned, Mowgli grew into a lean, strong young hunter who was respected by every creature in the jungle, yet he sometimes sat alone and wondered where in the world he truly belonged. Mother Wolf, who loved him dearly, told him gently that he was a man, that Shere Khan still waited for him, and that he must one day live among men. Mowgli listened in silence, thinking of the old cave, and at last he agreed to go and see the village of men for himself.

At the edge of the village, a gentle woman named Messua caught sight of the ragged, barefoot stranger, and her face changed, for years before a tiger had carried off her small son and she had never stopped grieving. Half believing, half afraid to hope, she took Mowgli by the hand and led him into her house, where she gave him food, a bed and a new language to learn. Mowgli, who knew only that she was kind and that the roof kept off the rain, decided to stay a while and watch these strange people at close quarters.

Slowly Mowgli learned the strange customs of the village: how to speak the language of men, how to wear a cloth about his waist, and why people attached such importance to money, which seemed to him a most puzzling thing. Each morning he rode out on a buffalo's broad back to graze the herd with the other boys, and he soon discovered that the great horned beasts obeyed him as readily as any wolf. Though he sometimes missed the jungle with a sharp pang, the days passed pleasantly enough, and he told himself that he was learning something useful.

At dusk, when the herd had settled for the evening, Gray Brother, the eldest of the wolves who had grown up in Father Wolf's cave beside Mowgli, slipped silently out of the long grass and licked his old friend's hand. In urgent whispers he warned that Shere Khan, who had learned where the boy had gone, was lying in wait in the dry ravine below the village and meant to catch him when he came out in the morning. Mowgli listened with narrowed eyes, for he had no intention of letting the tiger choose the hour of the fight.

Mowgli thought for a moment, and then he smiled, for he had remembered that no tiger, however fierce, could withstand the weight of a hundred frightened buffaloes thundering down a narrow valley. He sent Gray Brother to bring old Akela, and when the grey wolf arrived, the three of them laid their plan in whispers, deciding that the herd would be divided and driven into the ravine from both ends. By midnight the plan was settled, and Mowgli lay down beside the buffaloes to wait for the dawn.

At first light Mowgli climbed onto Rama, the great bull who led the herd, and with the wolves racing alongside, he guided the buffaloes to the head of the ravine, a long, deep gully with steep sides. There Akela and Gray Brother cut the herd in two, so that one half could be driven in from above while the other half blocked the far end. Not a creature made a sound, and the only movement in the dry valley was the thin dust rising from the hooves of the waiting animals.

Mowgli threw back his head and shouted the tiger's name into the ravine, and at the sound the herd poured down the narrow valley like a flood of horns and dust, shaking the very rocks with its fury. Shere Khan, trapped between the two halves of the herd with steep walls on either side, had nowhere to turn, and his long hunt for the man-cub ended there. When the dust had settled and the thunder had died, the ravine was silent, and the old fear of the jungle had gone.

In the silence that followed, Mowgli climbed down into the ravine, drew his knife as he had seen the hunters do, and took the great striped skin from the fallen tiger without a trace of triumph or fear. He had sworn on the night he left the Pack that this hide would one day lie upon the Council Rock, and now the oath could be kept. The buffaloes wandered peacefully away along the valley, and the wolves watched from the heights above.

Back at the village, a boastful hunter, who had hoped to claim the dead tiger for himself, recognised the great skin and began to shout that the boy was a sorcerer who spoke with beasts. Frightened and ignorant, the villagers took up the cry, shut their doors against Mowgli and threw stones at him as he passed, until he was forced to run for the safety of the trees. Messua wept at her door, but she was powerless to help him, and the boy she had hoped to call her son vanished into the dusk.

Mowgli stood for a long moment at the edge of the fields with a tight feeling in his chest, for he had hoped to find a home among men and had found only fear. Then he swung the heavy skin over his shoulder, turned his back on the lamps of the village and strode away into the dark. The jungle, whatever its dangers, had always been honest with him, and it was there that his footsteps now led him.

Mowgli reached the Council Rock before the sun was high, and he laid the great striped hide upon the stone, pinning it down at the corners with heavy sticks, exactly as he had once sworn that he would. Then he lifted up his voice and called the Pack to a meeting, and the wolves of the Seeonee came streaming down from the hills in the early light. Akela was among the first of them, and he looked at the skin for a long time and said nothing.

The wolves of the Pack crowded round the skin, sniffing and whispering, and then a great cry of welcome rose from them as they begged Mowgli to come back and to lead them in the place of the ageing Akela. Mowgli, who understood that power is a heavy burden, thanked them warmly but refused, saying that he would sooner run among his brothers than rule over them. Then, because the night belonged to singing, he sang a song of Shere Khan's death, and the whole hillside listened.

And so the boy who had been carried into a wolf's cave as a naked baby ran once more with the Pack through the silver forest, a creature who belonged to the jungle by choice as well as by upbringing. Shere Khan, who had hunted him since his infancy, was gone for ever, and Baloo, Bagheera, Kaa and Mother Wolf were close by to welcome him home. Where the river bent beneath the moon, Mowgli threw back his head and answered the calls of the night, and the whole jungle knew that its man-cub had come back to stay.
